hints: Focus on where the positive charge ends up after the first bromine attaches to the double bond, that carbocation decides the stability.
Draw each alkene quickly and see if adding Br to one end leaves a primary, secondary or tertiary positive carbon.
Remember the stability order tertiary > secondary > primary due to electron donation, so look for the alkene that can form a carbon with three alkyl groups around the $C^+$.
walkthrough:
**Recall how the cation forms**

Think of $Br_2$ as $Br^+$ plus $Br^-$. The $Br^+$ acts as the electrophile and adds to the $C=C$ bond first.

This leaves a carbocation on the other carbon: $C=C + Br^+ \rightarrow C(Br)-C^+$

**Link stability to substitution**

Carbocations are stabilised by alkyl groups pushing electron density toward the positive charge.

Stability order is:
$$tertiary \; (3 \; alkyl) > secondary \; (2 \; alkyl) > primary \; (1 \; alkyl)$$

**Compare the four alkenes**

Ethene, $CH_2=CH_2$, can only give a primary cation, $CH_2Br-CH_2^+$.

Propene, $CH_3CH=CH_2$, and 3,3-dimethylpent-1-ene, $CH_2=CH-C(CH_3)_2CH_2CH_3$, both give a secondary cation when $Br^+$ adds to the terminal $CH_2$.

**Spot the tertiary cation**

Methylpropene is $(CH_3)_2C=CH_2$. Adding $Br^+$ to the $CH_2$ end puts the positive charge on the more substituted carbon:
$$ (CH_3)_2C=CH_2 + Br^+ \rightarrow (CH_3)_2C^+-CH_2Br $$
That is a tertiary carbocation, the most stable of all the options.

options.A: 3,3-dimethylpent-1-ene is $CH_2=CH-C(CH_3)_2CH_2CH_3$. $Br^+$ adds to C1 to give $CH_2Br-CH^+-C(CH_3)_2CH_2CH_3$, a secondary cation. It is more stable than primary but less stable than tertiary.
options.B: Ethene is $CH_2=CH_2$. It gives $CH_2Br-CH_2^+$, a primary carbocation with only one alkyl group. This is the least stable type, so it is a common trap if you forget to count alkyl groups.
options.C: Methylpropene is $(CH_3)_2C=CH_2$. Addition of $Br^+$ to the $CH_2$ carbon gives $(CH_3)_2C^+-CH_2Br$, a tertiary carbocation stabilised by three methyl groups. This is the most stable intermediate.
options.D: Propene is $CH_3CH=CH_2$. $Br^+$ adds to the terminal carbon to give $CH_3CH^+-CH_2Br$, a secondary carbocation. It is stable, but a secondary cation is less stable than a tertiary one.
